Since $p$ divides no element of $S$, primality forces $p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$, so $p/1$ divides one of the original fractions; hence its image remains prime. Every nonzero nonunit fraction therefore factors into prime images. Matching prime factors successively gives uniqueness up to units and order, so $S^{-1}R$ is a UFD.

AA:530.statement: Let $\alpha\ne0$ be algebraic over a field $F$, with minimal polynomial $m_\alpha(x)=x^n+a_{n-1}x^{n-1}+\cdots+a_1x+a_0$. AA:530.canonicalSolution:
If $a_0=0$, then $x$ divides the irreducible polynomial $m_\alpha$. Irreducibility would force $m_\alpha=x$, contradicting $\alpha\ne0$; hence $a_0\ne0$. Reverse the coefficients to obtain $m_\alpha^*(x)=x^nm_\alpha(x^{-1})=1+a_{n-1}x+\cdots+a_1x^{n-1}+a_0x^n$. Evaluating at $\alpha^{-1}$ gives $(\alpha^{-1})^nm_\alpha(\alpha)=0$. The reciprocal of a nontrivial factorization of $m_\alpha^*$ would give a nontrivial factorization of $m_\alpha$, so $m_\alpha^*$ is irreducible. Its leading coefficient is $a_0$, and therefore $a_0^{-1}m_\alpha^*$ is the minimal polynomial of $\alpha^{-1}$. Also $\alpha^{-1}\in F(\alpha)$ and $\alpha=(\alpha^{-1})^{-1}\in F(\alpha^{-1})$, proving equality of the generated fields and hence equality of degrees. For $\alpha=1+\sqrt2$, the minimal polynomial is $x^2-2x-1$, whose monic reciprocal is $x^2+2x-1$; indeed $\alpha^{-1}=\sqrt2-1$.

Eisenstein gives $L\cong\mathbb Q[x]/(x^3-2)$, so base change yields $L\otimes_{\mathbb Q}L\cong L[x]/(x^3-2)$. In $L[x]$, $x^3-2=(x-\alpha)(x^2+\alpha x+\alpha^2)$. The quadratic has no root in $L$: a root $b$ would make $b/\alpha\in\mathbb R$ a root of $t^2+t+1$, impossible. It is therefore irreducible. The two displayed factors are coprime because the quadratic takes the nonzero value $3\alpha^2$ at $\alpha$. CRT now gives $L[x]/(x^3-2)\cong L\times L[x]/(x^2+\alpha x+\alpha^2)$. The second quotient maps isomorphically to $L(\omega)$ by sending the class of $x$ to $\alpha\omega$; its degree over $L$ is $2$, whereas the first factor has degree $1$. Under the product description, $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ are nonzero and have product zero.
